**Project: Midterm Datasprint**
**Name: William Burgett-Merkel**

**Introduction**
This dataset is the observations of Numbats in Australia. The reason this dataset exists is because Numbats are an endangered species, and tracking observations is important to ensure their habitat is protected. The main variables are the species name, latitude, longitude, the date and time of the observations, the day of the week the observation occured, the maximum and minimum temperature in celsius of the day the Numbat was observed, and precipitation that day in millimeters. 

I wanted to answer 3 questions from this dataset.
1. Where do the observations occur that actually have temperature data, and why only these observations?
2. What season are Numbats spotted most frequently and how are temperatures changing in these seasons by year?
3. Are there more cool or warm day observations?

**Analysis**
```{r}

#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

Get the data and then filter out any rows that do not have temperature values. Then create a column for what season the month occurred in based on Australian Climate. Finally plot the sightings with temperature data based on location in Australia.

```{r}
numbats <- read_csv("data/numbats.csv")

numbats_filtered<-numbats |> 
  filter(!is.na(tmax))

numbats_filtered<-numbats_filtered |> 
  filter(!is.na(tmin))

kable(head(numbats_filtered))

numbats_seasons<-numbats_filtered
  seasons<- c(
    "Dec" = "Summer", "Jan" = "Summer", "Feb" = "Summer",
    "Mar" = "Fall", "Apr" = "Fall", "May" = "Fall",
    "Jun" = "Winter", "Jul" = "Winter", "Aug" = "Winter",
    "Sep" = "Spring", "Oct" = "Spring", "Nov" = "Winter"
  )
  numbats_seasons$Season<-seasons[numbats_filtered$month]

australia_map <- map_data("world", region = "Australia")

ggplot()+
geom_polygon(data=australia_map,
              aes(x = long,
                  y = lat,
                  group = group))+

geom_point(data = numbats_seasons,
       aes(x=decimalLongitude,
           y=decimalLatitude,
           color=Season))+

  coord_quickmap(xlim=c(110, 122.5),
                 ylim=c(-40,-27.5))
```
Take the original dataset, filter out any rows that did not have a month in it, set the seasons based on Australia climate, and get the total observations in each season.
```{r}
numbats_filtered_all<-numbats |> 
  filter(!is.na(month))

numbats_seasons_all<-numbats_filtered_all
  seasons<- c(
    "Dec" = "Summer", "Jan" = "Summer", "Feb" = "Summer",
    "Mar" = "Fall", "Apr" = "Fall", "May" = "Fall",
    "Jun" = "Winter", "Jul" = "Winter", "Aug" = "Winter",
    "Sep" = "Spring", "Oct" = "Spring", "Nov" = "Winter")
  
  numbats_seasons_all$Season<-seasons[numbats_filtered_all$month]

numbats_seasons_all_count<-numbats_seasons_all %>%
  count(Season)
```

Get the mean min and max temperature. Then plot the observations with the tmax as the x and tmin as y to see the overall days when the events occurred. Also get the count of observations in each season.

```{r}
numbats_mean_tmin<-numbats_filtered |> 
  summarize(mean_tmin=mean(tmin),
            mean_tmax=mean(tmax))

numbats_seasons_count<-numbats_seasons %>%
  count(Season)

ggplot(numbats_filtered,
       aes(x=tmax, 
           y=tmin))+
  geom_line(size=.5)+
  geom_point(size=.75)


```

Group the months into seasons, then plot the observations by season.

```{r}
ggplot(numbats_seasons,
       aes(x=tmin, 
           y=tmax,
           group=Season,
           color=Season))+
  geom_line(size=.5)+
  geom_point(size=.75)+
  labs(title="Temperature of Each Numbat Sighting Sorted by Season",
     x="Minimum Temperature (°C)",
     y="Maximum Temperature (°C)",
     color="Season")
  
ggplot(numbats_seasons[numbats_seasons$Season == "Winter", ],
       aes(x=tmin, 
           y=tmax,
           color=factor(year)
           ))+
  geom_line(size=.5)+
  geom_point(size=.75)+
   labs(title="Temperature of Each Numbat Sighting in Winter",
     x="Minumum Temperature (°C)",
     y="Maximum Temperature (°C)",
     color="Year")

ggplot(numbats_seasons[numbats_seasons$Season == "Spring", ],
       aes(x=tmin, 
           y=tmax,
           color=factor(year)))+
  geom_line(size=.5)+
  geom_point(size=.75)+
  labs(title="Temperature of Each Numbat Sighting in Spring",
     x="Minimum Temperature (°C)",
     y="Maximum Temperature (°C)",
     color="Year")

ggplot(numbats_seasons[numbats_seasons$Season == "Summer", ],
       aes(x=tmin, 
           y=tmax,
           color=factor(year)))+
  geom_line(size=.5)+
  geom_point(size=.75)+
  labs(title="Temperature of Each Numbat Sighting in Summer",
     x="Minimum Temperature (°C)",
     y="Maximum Temperature (°C)",
     color="Year")

ggplot(numbats_seasons[numbats_seasons$Season == "Fall", ],
       aes(x=tmin, 
           y=tmax,
           color=factor(year)))+
  geom_line(size=.5)+
  geom_point(size=.75)+
labs(title="Temperature of Each Numbat Sighting in Fall",
     x="Minimum Temperature (°C)",
     y="Maximum Temperature (°C)",
     color="Year")
```
**Discussion**
1. All observations with temperature data points are tightly packed in a small area in Western Australia. This is likely because there is a more official reporting methodology in this location.

2. As I stated in #1, spring and winter were the most frequent season for observations in sightings that had temperature data. However, when looking at all sightings (as long as they had dates), winter and summer had the most observations with 235 and 217 sightings each, with spring and fall far behind them with 71 and 29 respectively.

3. There are more observations in cooler days, as there is a larger clump of data in lower tmin and tmax values. This correlates with the fact that winter and spring had the most observations.
